claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale precipitates, graded interfaces, and controlled phase distributions.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates stress transfer and dislocation motion during deformation.
A physics-informed ML surrogate can use high-rate mechanical-test data and TEM/APT-derived microstructural descriptors as inputs.
The proposed surrogate can reliably predict Young's modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can reliably predict yield strength for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can reliably predict fracture behavior, including fracture initiation or toughness, for HfNbTiVAl10.
The ML surrogate will be more accurate than conventional DFT or MD simulations.
The ML surrogate will be faster than conventional DFT or MD simulations.
The surrogate will reduce computational time by at least a factor of five.
The surrogate will achieve less than 5% prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Established simulations typically have prediction errors of 10–15% for the listed mechanical properties.
Explicit evaluation of fracture or yield strength in alloys is mostly beyond available DFT implementations.
DFT and classical MD require extensive computational resources.
Conventional DFT or MD simulations often fail to capture hierarchical microstructural effects accurately.
Correlating microstructural descriptors with macroscopic responses allows the surrogate to bypass computationally intensive atomistic simulations.
The HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure remains stable and its hierarchical features remain preserved from quasi-static to moderately dynamic loading near room temperature.
Significant microstructural evolution at very high strain rates or temperatures may cause the approach to fail.
Inadequate microstructural characterization may omit local failure mechanisms and degrade model performance.
The stated quantitative gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency have not yet been experimentally validated.
Crack nucleation and propagation may introduce complexities that the surrogate does not fully capture.
